title: Replaced Planks
question: A ship has every plank replaced one by one over years. Most people still call it the same ship. What are they tracking?
choices: The pattern persists despite new parts
correctAnswer: The pattern persists despite new parts
correctExplanation: Right. Identity is often assigned to an enduring arrangement rather than to the material that fills it.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the pattern persists despite new parts. The arrangement and history continue even as the stuff is swapped.
lessonContent:
Identity can attach to form, not matter.
Arrangement can outlast ingredients.
Notice what stays constant through change.
Distinguish stuff from structure.
Share this: name one thing whose identity survives its parts changing.

title: Thread of Memory
question: One theory says you are the same person over time because of what kind of link?
correctAnswer: Continuity of memory and character
correctExplanation: Right. On this view, psychological connections carry identity forward even as the body changes.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is continuity of memory and character. The thread is mental rather than material, which is why amnesia raises hard questions.
lessonContent:
Identity may rest on connections over time.
Psychological links can carry a person forward.
Material sameness is not required.
Ask what kind of continuity matters.
Share this: note one thing you carry forward from your past self.

title: Invisible Drift
question: Why can a person change enormously over decades without noticing any single leap?
choices: Change happens only in sudden jumps
correctAnswer: Gradual replacement makes change invisible
correctExplanation: Right. Small daily shifts escape notice, yet their sum can be transformative.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is gradual replacement makes change invisible. Slow drift hides itself, which is why sudden comparisons surprise us.
lessonContent:
Slow change evades daily notice.
Accumulated small shifts become large.
Compare across time, not day to day.
Look for gradual drift in yourself.
Share this: compare an old photo or note with your present self.

title: No Permanent Self
question: The bundle theory holds that what we call the self is really a collection of what?
correctAnswer: Changing experiences and mental states
correctExplanation: Right. On this view there is no core owner behind experience, only the bundle of experiences themselves.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is changing experiences and mental states. The sense of a unified self may be a pattern rather than a thing.
lessonContent:
Some theories deny a core owner.
Experiences may be all there is to a self.
Unity can be a pattern, not a substance.
Question what seems obvious.
Share this: observe for a minute the stream of your own experience.

title: Life as Story
question: The narrative view of the self says personal identity is shaped mainly by what?
choices: The story we tell about ourselves
correctAnswer: The story we tell about ourselves
correctExplanation: Right. Coherence comes from a narrative that links past, present, and future into one arc.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the story we tell about ourselves. Meaning and continuity are constructed through the accounts we build.
lessonContent:
Narratives create coherence over time.
We link events into a story.
Identity may be authored, not fixed.
Notice the plot you live by.
Share this: tell one chapter of your life in three sentences.

title: Same Body
question: Why does bodily continuity alone fail to fully explain personal identity?
choices: It is neither necessary nor sufficient
It has no connection to identity
correctAnswer: It is neither necessary nor sufficient
correctExplanation: Right. We can imagine psychological continuity without the same body, and bodily continuity without the same person.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is neither necessary nor sufficient. Thought experiments show the body can be neither required nor enough on its own.
lessonContent:
Single criteria often prove incomplete.
Thought experiments test necessity and sufficiency.
Consider whether a factor is required or enough.
Weigh several criteria together.
Share this: test whether one condition is required or merely helpful.

title: What It Is
question: What do philosophers call the properties without which a thing would no longer be itself?
correctAnswer: Essential properties
correctExplanation: Right. These define what kind of thing it is, as opposed to traits it merely happens to have.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is essential properties. Their loss changes the thing's identity, unlike traits that can come and go.
lessonContent:
Some traits define, others merely accompany.
Distinguish the necessary from the incidental.
Ask what could change without loss of identity.
Test by imagining removal.
Share this: name one property you would call essential to something you value.

title: Change Without Loss
question: Which kinds of traits can change while a thing remains itself?
correctAnswer: Accidental properties
correctExplanation: Right. Incidental features come and go without altering what the thing fundamentally is.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is accidental properties. A haircut or a new address does not change personal identity, while some changes would.
lessonContent:
Not every change is identity-changing.
Separate the incidental from the defining.
Ask what could vary without loss.
Use imagination to test the boundary.
Share this: list three things about you that could change without changing you.

title: Slow Versus Sudden
question: Why do we accept slow change as preserving identity but resist an instant total swap?
choices: Continuity of process is preserved slowly
Identity has no relation to time
correctAnswer: Continuity of process is preserved slowly
correctExplanation: Right. An unbroken path of change feels like one continuing thing, unlike a sudden replacement.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is continuity of process is preserved slowly. Continuity itself, not the amount of change, seems to do the work.
lessonContent:
Continuity can matter more than magnitude.
An unbroken process preserves identity.
A break feels like a different thing.
Ask whether the path was continuous.
Share this: notice one gradual change you accepted without alarm.

title: Perfect Copy
question: A perfect duplicate of you appears. Why do most people deny it is you?
choices: A copy is not the original
correctAnswer: A copy is not the original
correctExplanation: Right. Exact similarity is not the same as being the continuing original thing.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a copy is not the original. Sameness of features does not establish sameness of history and continuity.
lessonContent:
Similarity is not identity.
Duplicates share traits but not history.
Continuity of origin matters.
Distinguish looks from lineage.
Share this: name one thing that can be copied without being the same thing.

title: Copy and Erase
question: A machine copies you exactly, then destroys the original. Does the copy continue you?
choices: It tests whether continuity or pattern matters
It proves identity is only physical
correctAnswer: It tests whether continuity or pattern matters
correctExplanation: Right. The scenario isolates what we value: an unbroken path or the information pattern itself.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it tests whether continuity or pattern matters. Intuitions differ, which shows how contested the criteria are.
lessonContent:
Thought experiments isolate hidden commitments.
Your answer reveals what you truly value.
Conflicting intuitions signal deep questions.
Use puzzles to probe principles.
Share this: ask someone whether a perfect copy would be them.

title: Matter Swap
question: Why does complete material replacement not automatically destroy identity for many people?
choices: Sameness of arrangement outweighs sameness of stuff
Identity is only a legal fiction
correctAnswer: Sameness of arrangement outweighs sameness of stuff
correctExplanation: Right. The organization and history can persist even when the underlying material is entirely new.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is sameness of arrangement outweighs sameness of stuff. Structure, not substance, carries much of what we call identity.
lessonContent:
Organization can outrank material.
Structure carries information forward.
Separate pattern from substance.
Ask what must be preserved.
Share this: find one system whose pattern matters more than its parts.

title: Self as Process
question: Some philosophers say the self is better understood as what kind of thing?
choices: A process rather than a fixed object
A simple label with no reality
correctAnswer: A process rather than a fixed object
correctExplanation: Right. On this view, identity is an ongoing activity of maintaining and revising oneself, like a flame rather than a stone.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a process rather than a fixed object. Persistence becomes continuity of activity, not the endurance of a static thing.
lessonContent:
Some things persist by renewing, not by staying still.
A flame is the same while always changing.
Processes can have identity too.
Choose the right category for a phenomenon.
Share this: name one thing that persists by constantly renewing.

title: Seen by Others
question: What does the social dimension of identity depend on?
choices: Recognition and roles assigned by others
correctAnswer: Recognition and roles assigned by others
correctExplanation: Right. Part of who we are is sustained by how others see and treat us.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is recognition and roles assigned by others. Identity is partly relational, not purely an inner fact.
lessonContent:
Identity has a social face.
Recognition by others shapes who we are.
Roles are assigned and adopted.
Consider the relational dimension.
Share this: notice one part of who you are that others help sustain.

title: More Than Looks
question: Why do we treat character as more central to identity than appearance?
choices: Appearance has no cause at all
correctAnswer: Character shapes choices and relationships
correctExplanation: Right. Traits that guide action and connection seem to define a person more deeply than surface features.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is character shapes choices and relationships. What we do and how we relate carries more weight than how we look.
lessonContent:
We rank some traits as more central.
Conduct and relationships define a person.
Surface features matter less.
Ask what you would least want changed.
Share this: name one character trait you consider central to you.

title: Gaps in Memory
question: What challenge do memory lapses pose for the psychological view of identity?
choices: Memory has no role in identity
correctAnswer: Breaks in memory threaten continuity
correctExplanation: Right. If identity depends on remembered connections, gaps make the thread harder to trace.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is breaks in memory threaten continuity. This is why some theories loosen the requirement to allow overlapping chains.
lessonContent:
Any criterion faces hard cases.
Gaps test a theory's limits.
Loosen requirements when needed.
Revise the theory to fit the evidence.
Share this: consider how a gap would change one of your life stories.

title: Same River
question: Heraclitus noted you cannot step twice into the same river. What does this illustrate?
choices: Identity can endure through constant flow
correctAnswer: Identity can endure through constant flow
correctExplanation: Right. The river keeps its name and course even though the water is always new.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is identity can endure through constant flow. Change and persistence can be two sides of the same phenomenon.
lessonContent:
Persistence can coexist with change.
Names can track a flowing process.
Do not equate sameness with stillness.
Hold constancy and change together.
Share this: name one thing that stays itself while always changing.

title: In Between
question: Some philosophers suggest personal identity can come in what form rather than all-or-nothing?
choices: Degrees, with stronger or weaker links
correctAnswer: Degrees, with stronger or weaker links
correctExplanation: Right. Continuity can be stronger or weaker, as when memory connections thin out over time.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is degrees, with stronger or weaker links. Identity may be a matter of more or less rather than yes or no.
lessonContent:
Some properties admit gradations.
Persistence may vary in strength.
Reject unnecessary either-or framing.
Consider a spectrum.
Share this: find one yes-or-no question that is really a matter of degree.

title: Aims and Plans
question: What connects your present self to a future self even when traits change?
correctAnswer: Continued projects and intentions
correctExplanation: Right. Ongoing commitments and goals give a practical thread from present to future.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is continued projects and intentions. Responsibility and planning depend on this forward-looking connection.
lessonContent:
Projects link present and future.
Intentions carry responsibility across time.
Practical identity looks forward.
Notice what you are committed to completing.
Share this: name one long-term project that defines your future self.

title: Given and Made
question: How do many philosophers describe the sources of personal identity?
correctAnswer: Partly given and partly chosen
correctExplanation: Right. Circumstances and history set the starting point, while choices revise who we become.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is partly given and partly chosen. Neither total determinism nor unlimited self-invention captures the reality.
lessonContent:
Some conditions are inherited.
Choices revise what is given.
Avoid both fatalism and pure will.
Work with the material you have.
Share this: note one given trait and one chosen trait in yourself.

title: Not Fixed
question: What does the developmental view of the self emphasise?
choices: Identity forms and changes over a lifetime
Identity is set once and never moves
correctAnswer: Identity forms and changes over a lifetime
correctExplanation: Right. Who we are develops through stages, experiences, and choices rather than arriving complete.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is identity forms and changes over a lifetime. Growth and revision are normal, not a failure of consistency.
lessonContent:
Development continues through life.
Identity is a work in progress.
Change is not betrayal of self.
Allow for growth.
Share this: note one way you have developed in the past five years.

title: Two Rival Views
question: What is the core disagreement between bodily and psychological theories of identity?
choices: Which kind of continuity is essential
correctAnswer: Which kind of continuity is essential
correctExplanation: Right. Both accept continuity; they differ on whether the body or the mind carries it.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is which kind of continuity is essential. The debate is about the right criterion, not the existence of continuity.
lessonContent:
Rival theories can share assumptions.
Locate the precise disagreement.
Compare criteria directly.
Test each with hard cases.
Share this: find the exact point where two views actually diverge.

title: What We Value
question: In identity puzzles, what do people usually care about preserving most?
choices: The continuing pattern of a life
correctAnswer: The continuing pattern of a life
correctExplanation: Right. What matters is that the life and its connections continue, not that the same matter remains.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the continuing pattern of a life. Values, memories, and relationships carry more weight than atoms.
lessonContent:
Puzzles reveal underlying values.
What we protect shows what we prize.
Patterns and connections matter.
Ask what you would refuse to lose.
Share this: name the one thread of your life you would most want preserved.

title: Real Change
question: Must a thing stop being itself in order to change genuinely?
choices: No, real change can occur while identity persists
correctAnswer: No, real change can occur while identity persists
correctExplanation: Right. Growth and change are compatible with remaining the same subject through time.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is that real change can occur while identity persists. Persistence does not require frozen sameness.
lessonContent:
Change need not erase identity.
Enduring subjects can develop.
Reject the idea that sameness means stillness.
Hold continuity and change together.
Share this: describe one way you changed while remaining yourself.

title: Beyond Practical
question: Why is the problem of personal identity more than a practical question?
choices: It concerns what we fundamentally are
It has no implications at all
It is settled by common sense
correctAnswer: It concerns what we fundamentally are
correctExplanation: Right. The puzzle reaches questions of nature and existence, not just convenience or convention.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it concerns what we fundamentally are. Practical labels may work, yet the deeper question of our nature remains open.
lessonContent:
Some questions run deeper than convention.
Practical answers may not settle metaphysics.
Ask what kind of thing a person is.
Follow a question to its foundations.
Share this: reflect on what you take yourself most fundamentally to be.
